strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why adversarial training can preserve clean generalization while exhibiting a substantial robust generalization gap.
The explicit decomposition into signal learning and noise memorization provides an interpretable candidate mechanism and a useful framework for studying training dynamics.
The MNIST and CIFAR-10 experiments provide suggestive observations about input-space flatness, particularly the divergence between training and test sensitivity.
weaknesses: The central analysis does not establish robustness on training data under the stated perturbation set. GTA uses the ground-truth signal direction and generates fixed, signal-only perturbations; training error is measured on these examples, whereas robust test error maximizes over the full ball. Indeed, under Theorem 4.1's claimed scales, replacing noisy patches by -c times themselves makes the training margin α³U-c³V negative for a sufficiently large constant c, while requiring a perturbation much smaller than δ. Thus, the proposed learned state can remain vulnerable on training examples, undermining its interpretation as robust overfitting under standard adversarial training.

The feature-learning proof contains consequential gaps. Appendix C.12 infers bounds on individual noise-weight norms from aggregate memorization without establishing the required upper bounds, and incorrectly treats cubic Gaussian forms as sub-Gaussian. Moreover, the stated constant-order clean and attacked margins are incompatible with logistic loss converging to zero unless additional growth factors are introduced. These issues affect the justification of Theorem 4.1.

Theorem 5.2 is false under its stated assumptions when robust training means robustness throughout the perturbation balls. Assumption 5.1 permits a distribution supported on two well-separated labeled points with a fragile clean classifier. Once both points appear in training, zero robust training error necessarily implies zero robust test error, contradicting the claimed constant test error. A condition controlling coverage or uncovered probability mass is missing. Appendix D also claims uniform approximation of a discontinuous classifier by continuous ReLU networks without resolving the discontinuities.

Theorem 7.1 is false as stated. A biased constant predictor has zero input-gradient flatness, yet with two classes having smooth input densities, population loss can exceed empirical loss because of random sampled class proportions, with probability approximately one half. The claimed bound allows no such sampling error. Appendix E retains additive density-estimation errors that do not justify the displayed gradient-only bound. Furthermore, Proposition 7.2 concerns robust versus clean population risk, not the train–test generalization gap.

The empirical evidence does not identify the proposed mechanism. Flatness near training examples is compatible with multiple explanations and does not demonstrate partial signal learning or noise memorization. There are no direct synthetic checks of the predicted feature dynamics or interventions separating these mechanisms. Training attack details, optimization of the reported gradient maxima, estimation of global flatness, and variability across runs are insufficiently specified for reproduction and reliable interpretation.

The originality and explanatory scope of the representation lower bound need clarification. Weakening linear separability to neural separability in an existential lower bound does not itself strengthen the result attributed to Li et al. (2022), and Appendix D still constructs linearly separable data. An existential worst-case complexity separation also does not establish that practical distributions require exponential models or that optimization selects CGRO classifiers.
